sentences.text: Kronosaurus was an extinct genus of short-necked pliosaurs that lived in the Eromanga Sea, an inland sea in what is now Australia.
These animals were giant carnivorous marine reptiles and represented the largest known plesiosaurs, living approximately 120 million years ago.
The genus name Kronosaurus means "lizard of Kronos" and refers to the animal's large size and possible ferocity.
The holotype skull of Kronosaurus is estimated to have been 1.31 meters long.
McHenry estimated that Kronosaurus had at least 35 presacral vertebrae, comprising thirteen cervical and five pectoral vertebrae.
Kronosaurus teeth were long, exceeding 7 cm, but lacked the cutting edges and distinctive tetrahedral shape found in Pliosaurus and Liopleurodon teeth.
The largest Kronosaurus individuals likely had rear flippers that created a wingspan exceeding 5 meters.
Specimen QM F10113 is the most complete known Kronosaurus and contains the fossilized remains of a sea turtle in its stomach.
Researcher McHenry estimated the maximum size of Kronosaurus at 10.5 meters and suggested that smaller specimens under 7 meters were juveniles or subadults.
Based on specimen QM F10113, the bite force of Kronosaurus is estimated to be between 16,000 and 23,000 newtons.
While the Late Triassic ichthyosaur Ichthyotitan is currently the largest known marine reptile, estimated to reach around 25 meters in length, Kronosaurus was still a formidable predator.
The first known specimen of Kronosaurus was received in 1899.
In 1899, a partial fossil was sent to the Queensland Museum by Andrew Crombie.
The genus Kronosaurus was formally described by Albert Heber Longman in 1924.
Kronosaurus possessed uniquely shaped teeth indicating it was specialized for hunting large prey, unlike most other members of its group.
Kronosaurus had large cone-shaped teeth adapted for eating large prey.
Fossil evidence indicates that Kronosaurus preyed on sea turtles and other plesiosaurs.
Large rounded bite marks were found on the skull of an Australian elasmosaurid (Tuarangisaurus) from the Albian, likely produced by an attack from a Kronosaurus.
Kronosaurus likely had a high metabolism or was endothermic, a trait suggested by its survival in the cold southern waters of Australia.
A 2019 study found that Kronosaurus possessed enlarged red blood cells that likely aided it during deep dives.
Kronosaurus had a short tail that likely served for stabilization or steering rather than propulsion.
A Kronosaurus mandible shows healed bite marks from a lamniform shark of the Cretoxyrhinidae family, indicating interspecific competition.
A juvenile skull shows bite marks from an adult, suggesting intraspecific aggression or potential cannibalism.
The type species of the genus Kronosaurus is Kronosaurus queenslandicus.
Phylogenetic studies since 2013 place Kronosaurus within the subfamily Brachaucheninae.
The Colombian species K. boyacensis was reclassified into the distinct genus Monquirasaurus in 2022.
Kronosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous period.
Kronosaurus lived during the Aptian to Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
The Eromanga Sea where Kronosaurus lived reached cold temperatures close to freezing.
The validity of the genus Kronosaurus has been questioned due to the fragmentary nature of the holotype specimen.
Two additional species proposed for Kronosaurus are now considered unlikely or belonging to a different genus.
Colin McHenry suggests the Harvard skeleton has eight extra vertebrae and lacks the bulbous sagittal crest found on the real fossil.
While Kronosaurus was initially estimated to reach 12.8 meters in length, recent studies suggest the actual length is likely only 9 to 10 meters.
